title: Bài thi cuối Cấp 5 – Luyện thi IELTS 6.5 → 7.5 (đề rút gọn kiểu IELTS)
intro: Đề rút gọn mô phỏng IELTS Academic, bao phủ toàn bộ 14 bài của Cấp 5. Gồm: Phần 1–2 Listening (2 phần, 18 câu, nghe MỘT lần, khoảng 25 phút); Phần 3 Reading (1 bài dài, 14 câu, 25 phút); Phần 4 Kiến thức Writing & Speaking (9 câu, 10 phút); Phần 5 Writing Task 2 (40 phút); Phần 6 Speaking (11–14 phút, ghi âm). Điểm tự động tính trên 41 câu của Phần 1–4: cần đạt ≥ 70% (≥ 29/41) – tương đương mức Listening/Reading khoảng 7.0. Writing và Speaking tự chấm (hoặc nhờ giáo viên/bạn học chấm) theo rubric 4 tiêu chí và so với bài mẫu; khuyến nghị đạt khoảng 6.5 trở lên ở mỗi tiêu chí trước khi lên Cấp 6. Làm bài trong điều kiện thi thật: không tra từ điển, không nghe lại, bấm giờ từng phần.

sections.h: Phần 1 – Listening Part 1: Đặt tour xe đạp (câu 1–8)
sections.intro: Bạn sẽ nghe cuộc gọi đặt tour đạp xe cuối tuần. Đọc câu hỏi trong 30 giây trước khi nghe. Câu 1–7: viết KHÔNG QUÁ HAI TỪ VÀ/HOẶC MỘT SỐ. Câu 8: chọn đáp án đúng. Chỉ nghe MỘT lần, không xem lời thoại.

lines.t: Good morning, Green Wheels Cycling Tours. Emma speaking.
Hi, I'd like to book one of your weekend tours, please. I was looking at the mountain route on your website.
Ah, I'm sorry, the mountain route is closed at the moment because of road repairs. It should reopen in July. But the river route is very popular, and it's a bit easier, too.
The river route sounds fine, then.
Great. Which date were you thinking of?
Saturday the tenth of May, if possible.
Let me check. Hmm, the tenth is full, I'm afraid. We do have places on Saturday the seventeenth.
The seventeenth works for us.
Lovely. Can I have your name, please?
Daniel Ashworth. That's A, S, H, W, O, R, T, H.
Thank you. And how many people will there be?
Originally there were four of us, but one of my friends has had to drop out, so it'll be three.
Three people. Now, will you need to hire bikes?
Yes, please. What are the prices?
Electric bikes are twenty-five pounds per person, and standard bikes are eighteen.
We'll go for the standard ones. We could do with the exercise!

Eighteen pounds each, then. The tour starts at nine. We used to meet outside the railway station, but it's so busy there now that we've moved the meeting point to outside the public library, just across the square.
Outside the library. Got it. Do we need to bring helmets?
No, helmets are included with the bikes. But do bring a water bottle. There's only one café on the route, and it gets very hot by midday.
Will do. Can I pay on the day?
Normally, yes, but for groups we now ask for payment online by the Thursday before the tour. I'll email you a link.
That's fine. Thanks very much for your help.

items.q: 1. Route chosen: the ___ route
items.e: Mountain route bị đóng (“closed… because of road repairs”) → chọn river route. Bẫy đổi phương án (Bài 1).

items.q: 2. Date: Saturday ___ May
items.e: Ngày 10 đã kín (“the tenth is full”) → 17. Bẫy đổi ý/hết chỗ.

items.q: 3. Surname: ___
items.e: A-S-H-W-O-R-T-H. Nghe đánh vần theo nhóm chữ cái.

items.q: 4. Number of people: ___
items.e: “Originally there were four… so it'll be three.” – thông tin ban đầu là bẫy.

items.q: 5. Bike hire: £___ per person
items.e: Hai mức giá: 25 (xe điện) và 18 (xe thường); nhóm chọn “the standard ones” → 18.

items.q: 6. Meeting point: outside the ___
items.e: Bẫy cũ – mới: “We used to meet outside the railway station… we've moved the meeting point to outside the public library”.

items.q: 7. Participants should bring a ___
items.e: Mũ bảo hiểm “included” → không cần; “do bring a water bottle”.

items.q: 8. When must the group pay?
o: On the day of the tour
Online by the Thursday before the tour
items.e: “Normally, yes [on the day], but for groups we now ask for payment online by the Thursday before the tour.” – “Normally… but now” là tín hiệu thay đổi.

sections.h: Phần 2 – Listening Part 4: Bài giảng về tre trong xây dựng (câu 9–18)
sections.intro: Bạn sẽ nghe một bài giảng. Câu 9–16: hoàn thành ghi chú, viết MỘT TỪ VÀ/HOẶC MỘT SỐ. Câu 17–18: chọn đáp án đúng. Đọc tiêu đề ghi chú trước khi nghe: Biology & growth – Environment – Strength – Problems (durability, joints, regulation) – Next week. Chỉ nghe MỘT lần.

lines.t: Good morning, everyone. Today I want to look at a material that's been used for building in Asia for thousands of years, but which is now attracting interest from architects all over the world: bamboo.

Let's begin with some basic biology. Although bamboo looks like a tree and is often described as wood, it's actually a type of grass. That explains one of its most remarkable features, which is how fast it grows. The fastest-growing species can add almost a metre of height in a single day under ideal conditions.

More importantly for builders, most species can be harvested for construction after three to five years, compared with several decades for hardwood trees. And because the plant regrows from its roots, harvesting doesn't require replanting.

This rapid growth is the main reason bamboo is seen as environmentally friendly. A bamboo forest absorbs a great deal of carbon as it grows, and if the stems are then used in buildings, much of that carbon stays locked up for the life of the structure.

Now, what about strength? Bamboo performs especially well under tension, that is, when it's being pulled rather than squashed. In fact, some engineers argue that, relative to its weight, its tensile strength compares well with that of steel. It's also flexible, which is why bamboo scaffolding has traditionally been used even on very tall buildings in parts of Asia.

So why isn't everything built from bamboo? There are three main problems. The first is durability. Bamboo contains a lot of starch, which makes it extremely attractive to insects, particularly beetles, and it's also vulnerable to fungi in humid conditions. Untreated bamboo may last only a few years.

Traditionally, builders dealt with this by soaking the cut stems in water for several weeks, which washes out some of the starch. Today, the most common method is to treat the stems with a solution of boron, which is relatively safe for people but toxic to insects.

The second problem is joints. Because each stem is hollow and slightly different in diameter, connecting the stems securely is far more difficult than joining standard pieces of timber or steel. Much of the innovation in modern bamboo architecture has focused on new ways of making these connections.

The third problem is regulation. Very few countries have official building codes for bamboo, which means that engineers and insurance companies are often reluctant to approve large bamboo structures, however well designed they are.
Next week, we'll look at how engineered bamboo products, made by pressing strips of bamboo together into boards and beams, are attempting to solve some of these problems.

items.q: 9. Biology: bamboo is actually a type of ___
items.e: “it's actually a type of grass” – cấu trúc Although… actually… báo thông tin quan trọng.

items.q: 10. Ready for construction after three to ___ years
items.e: “harvested for construction after three to five years” – “several decades” là của gỗ cứng (nhiễu).

items.q: 11. Performs especially well under ___ (being pulled)
items.e: “performs especially well under tension, that is, when it's being pulled”.

items.q: 12. Attractive to insects because it contains a lot of ___
items.e: “Bamboo contains a lot of starch, which makes it extremely attractive to insects”.

items.q: 13. Traditional treatment: soaking stems in ___ for several weeks
items.e: “soaking the cut stems in water for several weeks”.

items.q: 14. Modern treatment: a solution of ___
items.e: “treat the stems with a solution of boron”.

items.q: 15. Second problem: ___ between hollow stems are difficult
items.e: “The second problem is joints… connecting the stems securely is far more difficult”.

items.q: 16. Third problem: few countries have official building ___
items.e: “Very few countries have official building codes for bamboo”.

items.q: 17. According to the lecturer, why is bamboo considered environmentally friendly?
o: It never needs to be replaced.
It grows quickly and absorbs carbon.
items.e: “This rapid growth is the main reason… absorbs a great deal of carbon”.

items.q: 18. What will the lecturer discuss next week?
items.e: Biển chỉ đường cuối bài: “Next week, we'll look at how engineered bamboo products…”.

sections.h: Phần 3 – Reading: một bài đọc học thuật (câu 19–32)
sections.intro: Đọc bài “Never Too Late? Language Learning in Adulthood” (đoạn A–G) và trả lời 14 câu trong 25 phút. Câu 19–23: TRUE / FALSE / NOT GIVEN. Câu 24–27: chọn tiêu đề phù hợp cho các đoạn C–F (đoạn A đã dùng tiêu đề “The origins of a popular belief”). Câu 28–30: hoàn thành tóm tắt bằng từ cho sẵn. Câu 31–32: chọn đáp án đúng.

read.title: Never Too Late? Language Learning in Adulthood
read.text:
A. Folk wisdom holds that children soak up languages effortlessly, while adults struggle for years and never quite succeed. This belief is not simply a matter of anecdote. In the middle of the twentieth century, researchers proposed what became known as the critical period hypothesis: the idea that the human brain is especially receptive to language during childhood, and that this window gradually closes around puberty. The hypothesis was attractive because it seemed to explain a familiar observation: the immigrant parent who speaks the new language with a strong accent, while the children sound like locals within a few years.

B. The evidence for an age effect is clearest in the case of pronunciation. People who move to a new country as young children typically end up with an accent that native speakers cannot distinguish from their own, whereas those who arrive as adults rarely do. For grammar, however, the picture is more mixed. Large studies of immigrants have found that grammatical accuracy, measured after many years in the new country, does tend to decline with age of arrival. But the decline appears to be gradual rather than abrupt, continuing well into adulthood, and some researchers argue that this pattern is difficult to reconcile with a sharply defined critical period.

C. Moreover, being young is not an advantage at every stage of learning. In the early months of instruction, adults and teenagers often learn faster than young children. They can understand explicit explanations of grammar, use dictionaries and other resources, apply deliberate memory strategies, and draw on what they already know about their first language. Classroom studies comparing different age groups over the first year of study frequently show older learners ahead. The younger learners' advantage, where it exists, tends to emerge only after many years of exposure.

D. Why, then, do so few adults reach a native-like level? Biology may be part of the answer, but it is not the whole story. Adults usually receive far less exposure to the new language than children do. A child who moves abroad may hear and use the language for most of the day, at school and with friends, whereas a typical adult learner attends a few hours of classes a week and then returns to a home in which the first language dominates. Adults may also be more self-conscious about making mistakes, and some feel, perhaps unconsciously, that keeping their original accent is part of who they are.

E. Motivation also matters. Adults learn languages for many reasons: to advance their careers, to settle in a new country, to connect with a partner's family, or simply for pleasure. Studies of adult learners suggest that the type of motivation is a better predictor of persistence than age. Researchers often distinguish between learners who are driven mainly by external rewards, such as an exam result or a promotion, and those who feel a genuine connection with the people and culture associated with the language. The latter group tends to continue studying for longer, even when progress is slow.

F. In recent years, interest in adult language learning has also been fuelled by claims about its effects on the brain. Some studies have reported that people who have spoken two languages throughout their lives tend to show symptoms of dementia later than those who speak only one. Other studies, however, have failed to find such an effect, and whether learning a language later in life offers similar protection remains unclear. What is less controversial is that language learning engages memory, attention and social interaction, all of which are associated with healthy ageing.

G. For adult learners, the practical implications are encouraging. Rather than worrying about a closing biological window, they would do better to maximise their exposure to the language through listening, reading and conversation, and to make deliberate use of the analytical skills that give them an early advantage. They might also set goals that reflect their real needs: for most purposes, being easily intelligible matters far more than sounding exactly like a native speaker. The question, in other words, is not whether adults can learn languages, since millions demonstrably do, but what kind of success they should aim for.

items.q: 19. People who move to a new country as young children usually develop native-like pronunciation.
items.e: Đoạn B: “typically end up with an accent that native speakers cannot distinguish from their own” → TRUE.

items.q: 20. Research shows that grammatical accuracy drops suddenly for people who arrive after puberty.
items.e: “the decline appears to be gradual rather than abrupt” – mâu thuẫn với “drops suddenly” → FALSE.

items.q: 21. In the first year of classroom study, older learners often make faster progress than young children.
items.e: Đoạn C: “Classroom studies… over the first year of study frequently show older learners ahead” → TRUE.

items.q: 22. Young children learn grammar more effectively when they are given explicit rules.
items.e: Bài chỉ nói NGƯỜI LỚN hiểu được giải thích ngữ pháp tường minh; không nói gì về trẻ em học quy tắc → NOT GIVEN.

items.q: 23. It has been proved that learning a language in later life delays the symptoms of dementia.
items.e: Đoạn F: “whether learning a language later in life offers similar protection remains unclear” – mâu thuẫn với “has been proved” → FALSE.

items.q: 24. Paragraph C
o: A head start for older beginners
More than a matter of the brain
Uncertain benefits for the ageing mind
The rising cost of language classes
items.e: Đoạn C: ở giai đoạn đầu, người lớn học nhanh hơn trẻ nhỏ → “A head start for older beginners”.

items.q: 25. Paragraph D
o: A head start for older beginners
More than a matter of the brain
Uncertain benefits for the ageing mind
The rising cost of language classes
items.e: “Biology may be part of the answer, but it is not the whole story” → nguyên nhân không chỉ là sinh học (exposure, tâm lý).

items.q: 26. Paragraph E
o: A head start for older beginners
More than a matter of the brain
Uncertain benefits for the ageing mind
The rising cost of language classes
items.e: Động lực quyết định sự bền bỉ (persistence) → “What keeps learners going”.

items.q: 27. Paragraph F
o: A head start for older beginners
More than a matter of the brain
Uncertain benefits for the ageing mind
The rising cost of language classes
items.e: Lợi ích cho não (dementia) “remains unclear” → “Uncertain benefits for the ageing mind”.

items.q: 28. Summary: Evidence that age limits language learning is clearest in the area of ______.
items.e: Đoạn B: “The evidence for an age effect is clearest in the case of pronunciation.”

items.q: 29. Summary: For grammar, the evidence is ______.
items.e: “For grammar, however, the picture is more mixed.” – conclusive là từ trái nghĩa gây nhiễu.

items.q: 30. Summary: Most adult learners should aim to be easily ______ rather than to sound exactly like native speakers.
items.e: Đoạn G: “being easily intelligible matters far more than sounding exactly like a native speaker”.

items.q: 31. According to paragraph D, one reason adults rarely reach a native-like level is that they
o: start learning too late to understand grammar.
usually receive much less exposure to the language.
do not attend enough classes at school.
items.e: “Adults usually receive far less exposure to the new language than children do.” Phương án C không có trong đoạn D (động lực ở đoạn E và không so với trẻ em).

items.q: 32. What is the writer's main conclusion?
o: Adults should not try to learn a new language.
The critical period hypothesis has been completely disproved.
Adults can learn languages successfully if they set realistic goals and maximise exposure.
Learning a language is the best way to prevent dementia.
items.e: Đoạn G: lời khuyên tăng tiếp xúc, đặt mục tiêu thực tế; “not whether adults can learn languages… but what kind of success they should aim for”. B quá tuyệt đối; D bị bác ở đoạn F.

sections.intro: 9 câu kiểm tra chiến lược và ngôn ngữ của Bài 6–14.

items.q: 33. (Task 1 – line graph) Câu nào là OVERVIEW tốt nhất?
o: In 2010, coal produced 50% of electricity and hydropower 40%.
Overall, renewables are expected to replace coal as the main source, while the share of gas remains unchanged.
I believe solar power is the best energy source for the future.
items.e: Overview nêu xu hướng chính, không số liệu chi tiết, không ý kiến cá nhân (Bài 6).

items.q: 34. (Task 1) The number of visitors rose ___ 20,000, from 50,000 to 70,000.
items.e: rise by + lượng thay đổi; rise to + mức đạt tới (Bài 6).

items.q: 35. (Task 1 – bar chart chỉ có năm 2024 cho 4 nhóm tuổi) Câu nào ĐÚNG về cách mô tả?
o: Car use increased from 8% to 30% as people got older.
Car use was considerably higher among older age groups than among young adults.
Car use was more higher among older workers.
items.e: Biểu đồ tĩnh → so sánh, không dùng ngôn ngữ xu hướng; “more higher” sai ngữ pháp (Bài 7).

items.q: 36. (Task 1 – map) The old market was ___ and replaced by a shopping centre. (phá dỡ)
items.e: Động từ thay đổi trên bản đồ, bị động quá khứ (Bài 8).

items.q: 37. (Task 2 – Opinion) Thesis nào trả lời rõ “To what extent do you agree or disagree?”
o: This essay will discuss both sides of the issue.
There are many advantages and disadvantages.
While free fares may help a little, I largely disagree that they are the best way to reduce congestion.
items.e: Thesis phải nêu lập trường và mức độ đồng ý (Bài 9).

items.q: 38. (Task 2) Đề “Discuss both views and give your own opinion” BẮT BUỘC:
o: Chỉ trình bày quan điểm bạn đồng ý
Trình bày cả hai quan điểm và nêu ý kiến của bạn
items.e: Thiếu một phía hoặc thiếu ý kiến → Task Response bị giới hạn (Bài 10).

items.q: 39. (Bài 11) Nối tiêu chí Writing với điều người chấm tìm:
pairs: Trả lời đủ mọi phần, ý được phát triển
Đoạn rõ ràng, ý nối logic, liên kết tự nhiên
Từ vựng rộng, chính xác, đúng collocation
Câu đa dạng, phần lớn không lỗi

items.q: 40. (Speaking Part 1–2) Điều nào ĐÚNG?
o: Part 1 nên trả lời 1 từ để tiết kiệm thời gian.
Part 2 có 1 phút chuẩn bị và bạn nên nói đến khi giám khảo dừng (khoảng 2 phút).
Part 2 phải kể chuyện có thật 100%, nếu không sẽ bị trừ điểm.
items.e: Part 1: trả lời 2–4 câu (A–R–E); Part 2: 1 phút chuẩn bị, nói 1–2 phút; giám khảo chấm ngôn ngữ, không chấm tính xác thực (Bài 12–13).

items.q: 41. (Speaking Part 3) Sắp xếp thành câu suy đoán có rào đón:
w: It's hard to say for sure,
teachers will become more like coaches.
items.a: It's hard to say for sure, but I'd imagine teachers will become more like coaches.
items.e: Rào đón + suy đoán – ngôn ngữ chủ chốt của Part 3 (Bài 14).

sections.h: Phần 5 – Writing Task 2 (40 phút, tối thiểu 250 từ)
sections.intro: Viết bài trong 40 phút, không tra từ điển. Sau đó tự chấm theo rubric 4 tiêu chí rồi mới đọc bài mẫu band 8+ để so sánh.

write.task: In many countries, more and more adults are returning to education later in life. Why is this happening? Is it a positive or negative development? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.
write.model:
In many countries, it is no longer unusual to see people in their forties or fifties attending evening classes, enrolling in online degrees or learning a new language. In my view, this trend is driven mainly by changes in the job market and by greater access to learning, and it is a largely positive development for both individuals and society.

The most important reason for the trend is that careers have become far less predictable. Technology is transforming industries so quickly that skills learned at university may be outdated within a decade, and many workers have realised that they need to retrain in order to remain employable. A bank clerk whose role has been partly automated, for instance, may take a course in data analysis to move into a new position. At the same time, online platforms have made education much more accessible. Adults who could never have attended a full-time course because of work or family commitments can now study in the evening, at their own pace and often at a modest cost.

I believe this development is overwhelmingly positive. For individuals, returning to education can open up new career paths and improve financial security, but it can also bring considerable personal satisfaction and confidence, particularly for those who missed out on higher education when they were young. For society, a workforce that continues to learn is better able to adapt to economic change, which reduces long-term unemployment. Admittedly, studying alongside a job can be exhausting, and some adults may struggle to balance their commitments. However, these difficulties can be eased if employers offer flexible hours or financial support for training, as many forward-thinking companies already do.

In conclusion, the growing number of adult learners reflects both the demands of a fast-changing economy and the new opportunities created by technology. Provided that they receive adequate support, this trend benefits learners, employers and society as a whole.
rubric: Task Response: trả lời rõ CẢ HAI câu hỏi (Why? và Positive/Negative?), lập trường nhất quán từ mở bài đến kết bài, mỗi ý có giải thích và ví dụ cụ thể
Coherence & Cohesion: 4–5 đoạn, mỗi đoạn một ý trung tâm có câu chủ đề; liên kết bằng ý và quy chiếu (this trend, these difficulties), không lạm dụng Firstly/Moreover
Lexical Resource: từ vựng chủ đề chính xác (retrain, employable, accessible, workforce, flexible hours…), collocation tự nhiên, không lặp từ đề, ít lỗi chính tả
Grammatical Range & Accuracy: câu phức đa dạng (mệnh đề quan hệ, điều kiện, bị động, nhượng bộ) và phần lớn câu không lỗi mạo từ, số nhiều, thì
Độ dài 270–330 từ, hoàn thành trong 40 phút, có 3–5 phút soát lỗi

sections.intro: Nhờ bạn học hoặc giáo viên đóng vai giám khảo (hoặc tự đọc câu hỏi rồi ghi âm). Part 1: trả lời 2–4 câu mỗi câu hỏi. Part 2: 1 phút chuẩn bị, nói 1–2 phút. Part 3: trả lời 30–60 giây. Nghe lại bản ghi, tự chấm theo rubric rồi so với câu trả lời mẫu.

tasks.p: Part 1: Do you enjoy learning new things?
tasks.model: I do, although it depends a lot on what it is. I'm happiest learning practical skills that I can use straight away, like a new feature in a piece of software or a recipe I've seen online. Learning things purely for exams, on the other hand, has never really motivated me. I think that's partly why I've stuck with English for so long: I can see the difference it makes at work almost every day.

tasks.p: Part 1: How do you usually learn new vocabulary?
tasks.model: Mostly through a flashcard app on my phone. Whenever I come across a useful word or phrase, I add it with an example sentence, and then I review my cards for about fifteen minutes on the bus every morning. I used to just write long lists in a notebook, but I'd never look at them again, so the app has made a huge difference.

tasks.p: Part 2: Describe a course or class that you enjoyed. You should say: what it was, when and where you took it, what you learned, and explain why you enjoyed it.
tasks.model: I'd like to talk about a short public speaking course I took about two years ago at a training centre near my office. It ran for eight weeks, with one three-hour session every Saturday morning, and there were about fifteen of us in the group, mostly young professionals who, like me, dreaded giving presentations at work. Each week focused on a different skill. In the first few sessions we worked on basics like posture, eye contact and controlling our breathing, and later we moved on to structuring a talk, telling stories and handling difficult questions from the audience. What made it different from other courses I'd taken was that we spent almost the entire time actually speaking. Every Saturday, each of us had to give a short talk, which was filmed, and then we watched the recording together and received feedback from the trainer and the rest of the group. I found that terrifying at first, but it was incredibly effective, because you could see exactly what you were doing wrong, like speaking too fast or looking at the floor. As for why I enjoyed it, I think it was mainly the sense of progress. At the start, I could barely get through a two-minute talk without my voice shaking, but by the final week I gave a ten-minute presentation without notes, and I genuinely enjoyed it. The atmosphere was also very supportive, and I'm still in touch with several people from the group. Looking back, it was one of the most useful things I've ever done for my career.

tasks.p: Part 3: Is it harder for adults to learn new skills than for children?
tasks.model: In some ways, yes, but I don't think it's as simple as saying children are better learners. Children certainly have more time, and they're usually less afraid of making mistakes, which helps a lot with things like languages or sport. Adults, on the other hand, are much better at understanding why something works and at organising their own learning. The real difficulty for adults is usually practical: they're juggling work and family, so it's hard to find regular time to practise. So I'd say adults can learn just as effectively, provided they're realistic about their goals and consistent with their practice.

tasks.p: Part 3: How might education change in the next twenty years?
tasks.model: It's hard to say for sure, but I'd imagine education will become much more flexible and continuous. Rather than studying for one degree in your early twenties and then stopping, people will probably return to learning several times throughout their careers, often through short online courses. Technology will also allow lessons to be tailored to individual students, so a student who struggles with one topic can spend longer on it. That said, I don't think classrooms will disappear. Learning is a social activity, and young people in particular need teachers and classmates to stay motivated and to develop skills like teamwork.

rubric: Fluency & Coherence: nói liền mạch, ngập ngừng chủ yếu để nghĩ ý chứ không phải tìm từ; Part 2 nói đủ khoảng 2 phút; ý có trình tự và liên kết tự nhiên
Lexical Resource: dùng được từ vựng chủ đề học tập và cách nói tự nhiên (stick with, make a huge difference, looking back…), diễn đạt lại được khi bí từ
Grammatical Range & Accuracy: linh hoạt thì (hiện tại, quá khứ, used to, hiện tại hoàn thành, điều kiện, suy đoán), phần lớn câu không lỗi
Pronunciation: dễ hiểu suốt bài; giữ âm cuối; trọng âm từ và câu đúng; ngữ điệu tự nhiên, chia cụm hợp lý
Part 3: có khái quát, lý do, ví dụ và câu nhượng bộ/cân bằng; xử lý được câu hỏi vặn
